t: Operations on Tree: Simulating Lock, Unlock, and Upgrade
o: You maintain lock state over a rooted tree described by a parent array and answer three request types: lock an unlocked node for a user, unlock a node only when the requesting user owns its lock, and upgrade, which locks an unlocked node for the caller while force-unlocking every locked node beneath it, provided no ancestor is locked and at least one locked descendant exists. Take parent = [-1,0,0,1,1,2,2], so node 0 is the root, nodes 1 and 2 are its children, and nodes 3-6 are leaves: lock(2,2) succeeds; unlock(2,3) fails because user 3 does not own the lock; unlock(2,2) succeeds; lock(4,5) succeeds; and upgrade(0,1) succeeds because node 0 is unlocked, descendant node 4 is locked, and no ancestor of node 0 is locked, after which node 4 is freed and node 0 belongs to user 1, making a further lock(0,1) fail. With n up to 2000 and at most 2000 calls, even rescanning sizable parts of the tree per operation fits comfortably in the limits.
k: Ancestors of a node form a simple path through the parent array, so checking for a locked ancestor is just an upward walk.
Descendants require top-down traversal, so precomputed children lists make subtree scans straightforward.
Ownership is all the state you need: store the locking user per node and treat absence of an entry as unlocked.
Upgrade must validate all three conditions before mutating anything, since a failed call changes no state.

a.i: Keep one cell per node recording the owning user, with -1 meaning unlocked. Every operation then just reads and writes that array; for upgrade, verify ancestors by walking parent pointers and discover locked descendants by testing, for every locked node, whether num lies on its ancestor path. Nothing clever is needed at this input scale.
s: Store owner[v] = -1 for all nodes at construction.
lock: succeed and set owner[num] = user only if owner[num] is -1.
unlock: succeed and reset owner[num] only if it currently equals user.
upgrade: walk from num to the root and fail if any locked node appears.
Collect every locked node whose ancestor path contains num; if none exist fail, otherwise clear them all and lock num.
a.t: O(n^2) worst case per upgrade call since each of up to n locked nodes walks an O(n)-deep ancestor path; lock and unlock are O(1).
a.sp: O(n) for one owner entry per node.

a.n: Approach 2: Children Lists + Targeted Subtree Sweep
a.i: Precompute children adjacency once so descendants can be visited top-down. An upgrade validates the three conditions with an ancestor walk plus a DFS confined to the subtree of num, collects the locked victims along the way, and only then mutates state. lock and unlock become constant-time array or dictionary writes.
s: Build kids[p] = list of children of p from the parent array.
lock: succeed and record owner[num] = user only if num is currently unlocked.
unlock: succeed and clear the entry only if user matches the recorded owner.
upgrade: walk from num to the root and fail on any locked node found.
DFS the subtree of num gathering locked nodes; if none exist fail, else clear them all and lock num for user.
a.t: O(1) for lock and unlock; O(h + s) for upgrade where h is the tree height and s the subtree size (O(n) overall worst case), since only ancestors and the subtree are touched.
a.sp: O(n) for parent links, children lists, and the lock registry.

w: Lead with Approach 2: children lists turn upgrade into a targeted subtree sweep, and the ancestor walk comes free with the parent array. Pitfalls: upgrade unlocks descendants regardless of who owns them, a rejected operation must change nothing (validate all three conditions before mutating), and locked descendants are not the same as locked children. A likely follow-up is beating O(n) per upgrade: an Euler tour with a Fenwick tree over subtree ranges supports locked-count queries and batch clears in O(log n).
